blocks.text: I can identify common structures of plant cells and relate each structure to its function.
Tap each word to see what it means.

items.def: A subcellular structure made from cellulose fibres that strengthens the cell and supports the plant.
A subcellular structure that contains the green pigment chlorophyll, which absorbs light for photosynthesis.
A subcellular structure filled with cell sap that helps keep the cell turgid.
A chemical reaction that plants use to make glucose, taking place in the chloroplasts.
The net movement of particles from a low to high concentration, against a concentration gradient, using energy.

Plant cells also have **three additional structures**:
In a plant cell the cell wall is the outermost layer. The cell membrane is the second layer in.
Each subcellular structure has a specific function. First, the ones that plant and animal cells share:

items.def: Partially permeable: it lets some substances through but not others, and controls what enters and exits the cell. This keeps the internal conditions of the cell relatively constant.
Where protein synthesis takes place.
A jelly-like liquid containing salts and nutrients, where many chemical reactions occur.
Where aerobic respiration occurs. It contains the enzymes for respiration.
Controls the cell activities. It contains the DNA, which is the genetic material.
This is where photosynthesis takes place. It contains the green pigment chlorophyll, which absorbs light energy for photosynthesis.
On the very outside of the plant cell. It is made from cellulose fibres, and it strengthens the cell and supports the plant.

blocks.text: Specialised cells in plants are adapted to carry out specific functions. They have specific shapes and structures, including subcellular structures, that help them do a specific job. Here are five examples:

blocks.label: Watch out!
blocks.text: The palisade cell is a specialised cell. It is the type of cell used for the 2D plant cell model. And not all plant cells contain chloroplasts: root hair cells do not.
**Function:** to absorb as much light as possible for photosynthesis. Palisade cells are found at the top of leaves.

items.def: To absorb as much light as possible for photosynthesis. The more chloroplasts, the more sunlight can be absorbed.
So that they can be packed close together at the top of the leaf. The more palisade cells there are, the more light can be absorbed.

items.term: found at the top of the leaf
items.def: To absorb as much light as possible.

blocks.text: Guard cells are found on the **underside** of leaves. They open and close the **stomata**, which are little holes.
When the stomata are open, carbon dioxide diffuses into the leaf, and water vapour and oxygen diffuse out.
Stomata are located on the underside of leaves to limit the amount of water lost through evaporation.
Guard cells are adapted to their function in these ways:

items.title: In bright light
items.sub: Guard cells absorb water by osmosis and become turgid. This keeps the stomata open.

items.title: In low light
items.sub: Guard cells lose water and become flaccid. This makes the stomata close.

blocks.label: Why does this matter?
blocks.text: When the stomata are open, water can evaporate. When they are closed, water cannot leave, so this helps control how much water the leaf loses.
The outside surface of roots is covered in root hair cells. **Function:** to absorb water and minerals from the soil. Water is absorbed by osmosis. Mineral ions are absorbed by active transport.

items.def: To increase the surface area for absorption of water and mineral ions.
To store as much water as possible.
To release the energy needed for the active transport of minerals from the soil.

blocks.label: Do root hair cells have chloroplasts?
blocks.text: No. Photosynthesis cannot take place without sunlight, so there are no chloroplasts in root hair cells.
The xylem and the phloem run up the stem of plants. The **xylem** transports water upwards from the roots to the leaves, in one direction.

items.def: To strengthen the hollow tubes and provide support.

items.term: ends of the cells broken down
items.def: This forms long hollow tubes that allow water to move through.
Xylem cells contain no subcellular structures, allowing water to pass through freely.

blocks.text: The **phloem** transports glucose and amino acids up and down the plant.

items.def: They join the cells and have small holes that allow glucose and amino acids to flow through (translocation).
They contain many mitochondria, which release energy to help transport glucose and amino acids.
This allows more glucose and amino acids to flow through.

blocks.text: Xylem: {water}, upwards only. Phloem: {glucose and amino acids}, up and down.

items: Plant and animal cells have some common subcellular structures. Plant cells usually have three additional structures: the cell wall, chloroplasts and a large permanent vacuole.
Each subcellular structure has a specific function within the cell.
Specialised plant cells are adapted for their function: palisade cells, guard cells, root hair cells, xylem and phloem.
They each have specific features that enable them to carry out their functions.

flashcards.front: What is the cell wall made from, and what does it do?
flashcards.back: It is made from cellulose fibres. It strengthens the cell and supports the plant.
A subcellular structure that contains the green pigment chlorophyll, which absorbs light for photosynthesis. Photosynthesis takes place in the chloroplasts.
A subcellular structure filled with cell sap that helps keep the cell turgid.
A chemical reaction that plants use to make glucose, taking place in the chloroplasts.
The net movement of particles from a low to high concentration, against a concentration gradient, using energy.

flashcards.front: Name the three extra structures that plant cells usually have.
flashcards.back: The cell wall, chloroplasts and a large permanent vacuole.

flashcards.front: Where are palisade cells found, and why?
flashcards.back: At the top of leaves, so they can absorb as much light as possible for photosynthesis.

flashcards.front: Name three adaptations of palisade cells.
flashcards.back: Many chloroplasts; column shape so they pack close together; found at the top of the leaf.
They open and close the stomata (little holes on the underside of leaves).

flashcards.front: What happens to guard cells in bright light and in low light?
flashcards.back:
Bright light: they absorb water by osmosis, become turgid and keep the stomata open.

Low light: they lose water, become flaccid and the stomata close.

flashcards.front: What do root hair cells do, and how is each substance absorbed?
flashcards.back:
They absorb water and minerals from the soil.

Water is absorbed by osmosis; mineral ions by active transport.

Water, upwards from the roots to the leaves, in one direction.

Its cell walls are thickened with lignin.
Glucose and amino acids, up and down the plant.

flashcards.front: Do root hair cells contain chloroplasts?
flashcards.back: No. Photosynthesis cannot take place without sunlight, so there are no chloroplasts in root hair cells.

worksheet.title: Worksheet: Plant cells: common structures and specialised cells
worksheet.instructions: Write a short answer to each question. Use the words from the lesson.

questions.prompt: Which structure is the outermost layer of a plant cell? (two words)
questions.explanation: The cell wall is the outermost layer of the plant cell; the cell membrane is the second layer in.

questions.prompt: Which substance in the cell wall provides strength and support?
questions.explanation: The cell wall is made from cellulose fibres.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the green pigment in chloroplasts that absorbs light?
Which process do plants use to make glucose?
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis takes place in the chloroplasts and makes glucose.

questions.prompt: Which structure is filled with cell sap to help keep the cell turgid? (two words)
questions.explanation: The large permanent vacuole is filled with cell sap.

questions.prompt: Which specialised plant cells are found at the top of leaves to absorb light? (two words)
questions.explanation: Palisade cells are at the top of leaves so they can absorb as much light as possible.

questions.prompt: Which specialised plant cells open and close the stomata? (two words)
questions.explanation: Guard cells control if the stomata are open or closed.

questions.prompt: Root hair cells absorb water and ___ from the soil. Write the missing word.
questions.explanation: Root hair cells absorb water and minerals from the soil.

questions.prompt: By which process do root hair cells absorb water?
questions.explanation: Water is absorbed by osmosis; mineral ions are absorbed by active transport.

questions.prompt: Which tissue in the stem transports water upwards from the roots to the leaves?
questions.explanation: The xylem transports water upwards in one direction.

questions.prompt: Which tissue in the stem transports glucose and amino acids up and down the plant?
questions.explanation: The phloem transports glucose and amino acids up and down.

questions.prompt: Xylem cell walls are thickened with ___, which strengthens the hollow tubes. Write the missing word.
questions.explanation: Lignin strengthens the hollow xylem tubes and provides support.
